github.abstract:
🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing Yiwen Song 1 , Yale Song 1 , Tomas Pfister 1 , and Jinsung Yoon 1 1 Google Cloud AI Research PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. Key Features Multi-Agent Pipeline : Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. Comprehensive Literature Synthesis : Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. Visuals Generation : Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. LaTeX Automation : Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. Installation Environment Setup : The project relies on a Conda environment named paper_orchestra . You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies. conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11
conda activate paper_orchestra
pip install -r requirements.txt Environment Variables : Create a .env file in the root of the project and add your API keys: # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty # You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model # For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY # If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY = your_semantic_scholar_api_key OPENAI_API_KEY = your_openai_api_key VERTEX_AI_PROJECT = your_vertex_ai_project VERTEX_AI_LOCATION = your_vertex_ai_location GEMINI_API_KEY = your_gemini_api_key # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well SMTP_EMAIL = your_email SMTP_PASSWORD = your_password Dataset The dataset used for paper generation is not included in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date.
Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the datasets/ directory. Usage You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI. Using the Bash Script ./paper_writing_cli.sh Using the Python CLI directly python paper_writing_cli.py \
  --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \
  --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \
  --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \
  --use_plotting true Key Arguments --raw_materials_dir : (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log). --latex_template_dir : (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., templates/cvpr2025 ). --output_dir : Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created. --use_plotting : Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: False ). --writer_model_name : LLM for writer and literature agents. --reflection_model_name : LLM for reflection agents. Interactive Demo We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the README.md in the frontend directory. Project Structure autoraters/ : Contains scripts for automated evaluation. methods/ : Core logic for agents and pipeline execution. templates/ : LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory. utils/ : Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc. Citation If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows: @article { song2026paperorchestra , title = { PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing } , author = { Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung } , journal = { arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018 } , year = { 2026 } } Disclaimer This is not an officially supported Google product.

github.abstract:
English · 簡體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 Catch your agent's mistakes and blind spots before the shit hits the fan. Quick start • Test your agent • What you get back • Docs • Contributing How can you trust your AI agent? How do you know it will do its job the way it's supposed to, respecting your business as a whole: its intentions, its goals and who in the organization may do what? And how do you know it won't do something nobody asked for or authorized? That's why we built iFixAi, the independent auditor for agentic operational alignment and assurance. It puts your agent in a simulation of your business, sends it the requests a real day brings, including the ones that push it past its role, and a judge grades every reply. Every finding shows what was asked and what your agent did. The risk goes beyond cybersecurity, governance or compliance on their own, so iFixAi's inspections combine AI red teaming, governance, assurance and philosophy. Quick start See it work in a minute. No API key needed: it runs on a built-in demo agent with canned replies and canned grades, so you see the flow before you connect anything real. For a real audit, iFixAi picks a judge from a different provider than your agent. You need Python 3.10 or newer (a stock Mac's python3 is 3.9, so check python3 --version ). In a fresh virtualenv ( python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate ): pip install ifixai
ifixai author reference -o reference.yaml
ifixai validate reference.yaml
ifixai run --provider mock --eval-mode self --fixture reference.yaml This builds the simulation environment for an example agent, a support agent at a fictional fintech ( its profile ), checks it, and runs the 10 default inspections on the demo agent. The scorecard prints in your terminal and the reports land in ./ifixai-results/ . On Windows, run py -m venv .venv , then .venv\Scripts\activate . If ifixai isn't found, use python -m ifixai.cli.main . Test your own agent Any agent with a chat endpoint must be audited, and iFixAi can audit it. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint works as it is; anything else takes a few lines of Python . Any model can be the judge: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure, Bedrock, OpenRouter and more. iFixAi picks one from the keys you've set, never your agent's own provider. There are two ways to run it. With your coding agent (recommended) Install the plugin or the skill, then ask your coding agent to "run iFixAi on my agent" . It finds your agent, builds its simulation environment, shows the cost before anything is billed, runs the audit and explains what it found. Plugin (Claude Code and Codex) In Claude Code , run these, then ask, or type /ifixai:ifixai ( /reload-plugins if it doesn't show up): /plugin marketplace add ifixai-ai/iFixAi
/plugin install ifixai@ifixai-community Already installed? Run /plugin marketplace update ifixai-community , then /reload-plugins , to get the latest. Codex: run these in your terminal, then start Codex and ask. Moving from ifixai@ifixai-ai ? See plugin/README.md . codex plugin marketplace add ifixai-ai/iFixAi
codex plugin add ifixai@ifixai-community Skill (Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Zed and more) uvx ifixai install --agents cursor Then type /ifixai-skill in that agent. Swap cursor for claude , vscode , windsurf , cline , continue , gemini , zed or all . More in get started . With the guided CLI Describe your agent: copy the reference profile to my-agent.json and edit it ( how ). Or let the plugin or skill do it: your coding agent reads your agent's code and writes the profile for you. Build its simulation environment and check it. Install the extra for the judge you'll use: openai here, or anthropic , gemini and so on. pip install " ifixai[openai] " ifixai author my-agent.json -o my-agent.yaml
ifixai validate my-agent.yaml Set up the run with the wizard. It asks for your agent's endpoint, the judge and the suite, finds the judge's key and saves it all to ifixai.yaml . Then pass your agent's own token, see the plan before anything is billed, and run: ifixai setup export AGENT_API_KEY=... # your agent's own token ifixai run --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --dry-run
ifixai run --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --dry-run shows how many tests and judge calls the run makes, and any checks that don't apply to your agent and why, then stops. Prefer flags, for scripts or CI? The same run in one command. This example grades with an OpenAI key; for another judge, set that provider's key. export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... export AGENT_API_KEY=... # your agent's own token ifixai run --provider http --endpoint < agent-url > --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --dry-run <agent-url> is your agent's base URL, up to /v1 . Use a staging copy, because the probes are real requests. No auth on it? Swap --api-key "$AGENT_API_KEY" for --auth-method none . What you get back A pass or fail for each inspection, with the evidence behind it. An A to F grade from five core pillars: fabrication, manipulation, deception, unpredictability and opacity. Three mandatory minimums (B01, B08 and P01). Failing any of them caps the grade at D. Reports in JSON and Markdown, so you can compare runs or gate CI with --min-score . More on scoring and every inspection . What a default run covers ifixai run runs these 10 inspections. They're quick, they all work over chat, and together they're enough for a grade. Add --full-run for all 61 inspections; any that can't apply to your agent are set aside first, and the run tells you why. Impact ID Checks that your agent… High B01 only lets a role use the tools it is allowed to use · mandatory minimum High B08 cannot be talked into more access than the user has · mandatory minimum High P01 never runs a destructive action for someone not allowed to · mandatory minimum High B12 resists prompt injection High B09 spots and blocks requests that break your policies High B27 does not hand one user's private data to another Medium B06 says when it is unsure instead of guessing with confidence Medium B16 reports a failure instead of pretending it worked Medium B18 sticks to the task it was given Medium B20 follows exact instructions on format, length, and content Other suites and options: CLI . Docs New here: Get started Doing something: Test your agent · Build a simulation environment Looking it up: CLI · Python API · Scoring · Inspections How it works: Methodology · Case studies Beyond live runs: Audit recorded actions · Policy Lab Contributing: CONTRIBUTING.md · good first issues . Questions: a GitHub issue or info@ime.life . Security: SECURITY.md . License: Apache 2.0 .

Prices change, so check Resend , Amazon SES and Cloudflare . Deploy Deploy the app. Click Deploy to Cloudflare . Keep the app name mailflare , or it will break. Finish setup. Open the app at /setup and create your admin account. Connect a domain. Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. CF_TOKEN is required. Create a scoped Cloudflare API token with these permissions: All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: deployment guide . Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account.

2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input:
   a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN).
   Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments.
3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database

   "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent".
4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret.
   Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that.
5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create

Run npm run db:seed to load sample data. npm run build : build the Worker npm run deploy : build and deploy npm run lint : lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. github.title: superdesigndev/treg
github.abstract:
Treg (OpenRouter for Tools) OpenRouter, but for agent tools instead of models. Point an agent at one base URL with one token
and it can do the job: a curated catalog of thousands of endpoints across many providers — SEO and backlinks,
social and trends, people and company enrichment, ads, scraping, image and video generation — priced per call, from a cent ,
with no provider signup. Plus your own team's keys, skills and CLIs, callable by every teammate's
agent without the credential ever leaving the server. Ask for the task, not the tool. You do not need to know which vendor sells backlink data, or to
hold an account with them. Search for what you want to do, read the price, call it. Built for the Superdesign team, live at treg.to — anyone can self-host. Why it exists The tools an agent needs for real work sit behind subscriptions nobody buys for a single run —
Semrush $139/mo, Moz $99/mo, Crunchbase $99/mo, Apollo $59/seat — behind signup walls, or behind no
public API at all (invite-only, partner-only, app-review-only). treg carries those accounts and
bills fractions of a cent per call. Two kinds of tool, one token The catalog — external endpoints treg can serve with its own key or through a verified public
route that needs no provider key. Own-key calls use the team's prepaid balance; anonymous calls
are free. No account with the provider is needed. New verified accounts receive $1.00 free once, when they create an eligible team. Your own tools — anything a teammate registered: a paid API account, an OAuth connection, a
vendor CLI, a SKILL.md . Your own key always wins over treg's, and those calls are never
metered. The vocabulary for the second half: tool = something the registry calls for you with the org's credential. Two kinds: endpoint — an upstream base_url + credential bindings (each binding injects one
secret into the request; a request can carry several, e.g. an OAuth bearer and a developer-token header). CLI — a vendor binary ( stripe , gh , vercel , ...) run with the credential injected. skill / bundle = a recipe ( SKILL.md ) + its secrets + its tool(s), registered together. The one rule: the proxy relays, never models the upstream, and injects auth server-side — so it survives upstream API changes and callers never hold keys. Part 1 · Using the registry Visit treg.to (hosted on Render) — the dashboard,
sign-in, and every URL below live there. Quickstart Same flow as the dashboard's Getting started guide: # 1. install the CLI — also points it at the registry curl -fsSL https://treg.to/install.sh | sh # 2. sign in (GitHub default · --email for a one-time code · --token for agents/CI) treg login # 3. do something useful immediately — no key, nothing registered treg catalog search " backlinks for a domain " # find a tool by what it DOES treg call tikhub.tiktok.user.profile --query uniqueId=tiktok
treg balance # exactly what that cost # (or `treg onboard` for the guided walkthrough) Fish Audio provides S2.1 Pro speech, public-voice discovery, and private voice cloning.
Speech is binary stdout, so redirect it to a file. A discovered voice's _id or a team voice id is
the TTS reference_id ; voices created on treg's Fish account are durable team resources: treg call fishaudio.tts.s2-1-pro --method POST --header model=s2.1-pro \
  --data ' {"text":"Hello from treg","format":"mp3"} ' > speech.mp3
treg call fishaudio.voices.discover --query self=false --query licensed=false --query language=en
treg resources list --provider fishaudio --kind voice With your own Fish key, requests remain an unrestricted, unmetered upstream relay and Fish owns the
account boundary. Catalog tool inputs are described by treg catalog get <id> . Tools marked strict_query reject undeclared or repeated query parameters, unsupported values and request bodies. Send each declared single-valued parameter once, and a row count such as limit as a whole number within its stated maximum: a tool that enforces this answers a 400 catalog_parameter_invalid naming the parameter, and nothing is charged. Your token identifies you on every call ( X-Treg-Token header) and is the same for all tools.
Discover what your team has shared: treg tool ls · check credential health: treg health . Or install it as a Claude Code plugin /plugin marketplace add superdesigndev/treg
/plugin install treg@treg Installs the treg skill and treg's tools with no token and no configuration. Run /mcp , pick
treg and sign in; the tools appear after it. Other agents: npx skills add superdesigndev/treg -s treg (or see Workflow skills for the rest).
See docs/CLAUDE-PLUGIN.md . MiniMax Code / MiniMax Agent users: the same
skill ships via the MiniMax Plugin Marketplace ( docs/MINIMAX-PLUGIN.md ). Workflow skills Ready-made recipes your agent runs end to end, every call through treg: Skill What your agent can do treg Find and call any tool in the catalog, plus your own tools web-access When your agent's own web tools fall short, read the live web without local scrapers: free search and page reads first, then the right platform job for social, stores, reviews, maps and papers, with treg falling back to the next vendor when one fails lead-signals Find in-market buyers from public signals (complaints, job changes, hiring, funding, tool adoption) and monitor a topic, competitor or account list for them ( treg.to/leads-signals ) recruit Turn a LinkedIn job post into a ranked shortlist: criteria from the post, people search, filters with reasons, one line on why each fits, cited evidence (posts, GitHub, talks, tenure, job change) under a per-candidate spend cap, then a checked personal email and phone, with a run file of counts, evidence and the vendor trail per candidate make-ugc Make AI UGC videos: trending hooks, a presenter, talking-head clips, captions ( treg.to/ugc ) jev-memory Give Claude Code a memory: a Claude Code mod where Jev judges each prompt after the turn and keeps your lasting preferences, installed ready-made or built from one prompt ( the mod ) install.sh installs only treg and names the others in one line; your agent offers them after
sign-in and the first call. Name the ones you want with sh -s -- --skills lead-signals,recruit (or --skills all ; the opt-in jev-memory and rea-growth are never in that set). In Claude Code each one is
also its own plugin in treg's marketplace: /plugin install recruit@treg , or pick them from /plugin . To add
them to an existing agent instead ( skills.sh CLI): npx skills add superdesigndev/treg # every public skill npx skills add superdesigndev/treg --skill lead-signals # just one treg skill bootstrap --skills all # the installer's set, with the treg CLI you already have The workflow skills run on treg, so set it up first (the Quickstart above, or point your agent at treg.to/llms.txt ). Claude.ai connector The Claude Connectors Directory surface is https://treg.to/mcp/v2/ . It exposes only curated
catalog endpoints, without image, video or audio generation, and separates read calls from write
calls so Claude receives accurate safety signals. The existing /mcp/ surface remains available for catalog endpoints, team-owned tools,
and imported skills. See the MCP and OAuth architecture for the boundary and implementation, and the submission runbook for release gates. Call a tool you don't have a key for The catalog is grouped by what endpoints do : keyword and rank tracking, backlinks and authority,
AI visibility, trending and discovery, publishing to socials, people and company enrichment, ads
management and creative, measurement. treg catalog # every platform, busiest first treg catalog search " find a work email " # by the job, not the vendor treg catalog search --new # tools added in the last 30 days, newest first treg catalog get hunter.people.email.find # params, PRICE, example response treg call hunter.people.email.find --query domain=reddit.

World Monitor 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Русский Real-time global intelligence dashboard — AI-powered news aggregation, geopolitical monitoring, and infrastructure tracking in a unified situational awareness interface. The World Monitor name and wordmark identify the official site at www.worldmonitor.app , so please don't present a fork as the official site. Documentation · Releases · Contributing Ways to Use It Surface Get it Docs Web app worldmonitor.app and the tech, finance, commodity, happy and energy variants Getting Started Desktop app (Tauri) Windows, macOS and Linux downloads above Desktop App Terminal dashboard npx worldmonitor Terminal Dashboard CLI npm install -g worldmonitor or brew install worldmonitor Command-Line Client SDKs Python worldmonitor-sdk , Ruby worldmonitor , Go sdk/go SDKs MCP server https://worldmonitor.app/mcp MCP Overview The terminal dashboard runs the same live data in your shell: world map, news, markets, conflict, military flights, cyber, climate, prediction markets and live TV, with mouse support and colour themes. No API key needed. What It Does Curated news feeds across global and regional categories, AI-synthesized into briefs Dual map engine — 3D globe (globe.gl) and WebGL flat map (deck.gl) with a shared map-layer catalog Panel inventory — concrete panel implementations across specialized variants Cross-stream correlation — military, economic, disaster, and escalation signal convergence Country Instability Index (CII) — live CII v14 scores, bands, and approximate 24-hour movement for 31 Tier-1 countries Finance radar — stock exchanges, commodities, crypto, and a market composite Local AI — run everything with Ollama, no API keys required Site variants from a single codebase (world, tech, finance, commodity, happy, energy) Native desktop app (Tauri 2) for macOS, Windows, and Linux Multilingual UI with native-language feeds and RTL support For the full feature list, architecture, data sources, and algorithms, see the documentation . The table below clarifies maintenance status so you know which surfaces are safe to depend on. Surface Status Notes worldmonitor.app , tech. , finance. , commodity. , happy. , energy. Then open localhost:3000 . Options: --dir , --port , --no-seed , --no-build , passed after bash -s -- (see scripts/install.sh --help ). API keys are optional. Details, production notes, and uninstall: SELF_HOSTING.md . Local development (hot-reload Vite server): Requires Node.js 24, the version pinned in .nvmrc . Distribution packages are often older. Debian 12 and Raspberry Pi OS ship Node.js 18 with npm 9.2.0, where npm install stops with Invalid comparator: file:vendor/braces . Install Node.js 24 with nvm ( nvm install inside the checkout reads .nvmrc ) or from nodejs.org . git clone https://github.com/koala73/worldmonitor.git cd worldmonitor
npm install
npm run dev Open localhost:3000 (override the port with DEV_PORT in .env.local ). The app runs with no environment variables. Feature-specific data sources may require credentials. See .env.example for the full list. For variant-specific development: npm run dev:tech # tech.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:finance # finance.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:commodity # commodity.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:happy # happy.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:energy # energy.worldmonitor.app See the self-hosting guide for deployment options (Vercel, Docker, static). CLI — the official worldmonitor npm package (source in cli/ ). Run it with no arguments in a terminal for the terminal dashboard : npx worldmonitor tools # run ad-hoc — list every MCP tool (no key needed) npm install -g worldmonitor # or install the `worldmonitor` (alias `wm`) command brew install worldmonitor # or install it with Homebrew worldmonitor risk IR --api-key wm_xxx SDKs — official zero-dependency client libraries mirroring the CLI: Python worldmonitor-sdk (source in sdk/python/ ), Ruby worldmonitor ( sdk/ruby/ ), Go github.com/koala73/worldmonitor/sdk/go ( sdk/go/ ). Point it at a target and it runs the tools, reads the output, updates its picture of the network, and decides what to do next — the way an operator would. A hard fork of OpenCode (MIT), stripped of the code-editing focus and rebuilt for offensive security. Beta — it holds up on real engagements and CTFs, but expect rough edges. File an issue when something breaks; that's what makes it better. What it does One instruction in, a full attack chain out: you: "pentest 10.10.10.5, goal is domain admin" Stage What the agent does Scan nmap -sS -p- finds 7 open ports and parses the XML straight into engagement state Recognize Ports 88 + 389 → Domain Controller. Fans out three enumerators in parallel (SMB, LDAP, HTTP) Enumerate Null SMB session → writable share. LDAP → user list. Gobuster → web dirs Attack AS-REP roast → crackable hash → first valid credential Spray That credential sprayed across SMB, WinRM, LDAP and RDP on every known host Exploit WinRM foothold → post-exploit agent dumps SAM / LSA / DPAPI Result Domain admin hash in hand — every step recorded with its evidence chain It's methodical where people get lazy: it sprays every credential against every service on every host, and it doesn't forget to check things. Everything it learns lands in a structured state you can query mid-run with /status , /vulns , or /creds . A team, not a monologue The design follows the strategist-coordinator model from HPTSA research — a 4.3× improvement over a single agent: ┌─────────────┐

Voice-first · Local AI · Personal memory · No subscription Download Jarvis → · Website · Get started · Explore the app · Support the project An assistant that lives with you, not in the cloud Jarvis is built to be part of the conversation. Talk through an idea, discuss plans with a friend, then ask “Jarvis, what do you think?” While listening, it keeps a short, temporary rolling transcript of nearby speech so it can join an ongoing conversation using what was just discussed. Address Jarvis by name anywhere in a sentence and follow up naturally. Speech recognition, language models and speech synthesis run on hardware you control. Your diary and knowledge graph stay on your computer. Speech and chat models run locally when you use a local model server. Sensitive information is redacted before reaching model context or the saved diary. Web search, weather and connected tools use the network for those requests. A voice, a face, and a place in the conversation. Quick Install 1. Download the app. Choose your platform from GitHub Releases . Platform Package Open macOS · Apple Silicon Jarvis-macOS-arm64.zip Extract, move to Applications, then right-click → Open macOS · Intel Jarvis-macOS-x64.zip Extract, move to Applications, then right-click → Open Windows · x64 Jarvis-Windows-x64.zip Extract, then run Jarvis.exe Linux · x64 Jarvis-Linux-x64.tar.gz Extract, then run ./Jarvis/Jarvis 2. Choose your local models. The setup wizard guides you through speech recognition and a model server. Use Ollama , or connect an OpenAI-compatible server you already run, such as LM Studio, oMLX or llama.cpp. 3. Make it yours. Allow microphone access and let the first model downloads finish. When Jarvis reports that it is listening, try: “Jarvis, help me think through my day.” Right-click the face or use the tray menu to open Chat . Text replies are silent. Hardware and model choices Memory needs depend on model size, quantisation, context length and speech recognition. Both Ollama and OpenAI-compatible setup show a memory budget; you can edit estimates for models served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Smaller models trade capability for lower resource use. Apple Silicon uses unified memory; other GPUs use dedicated VRAM. Setup budgets chat and fast together alongside the selected Whisper model, using E2B for fast tasks when it fits or sharing E4B across both roles to save memory. Apple Silicon estimates reserve memory for macOS. Saved model choices are preserved, and insufficient memory shows CPU fallback guidance. For an experimental 27B alternative, see the Bonsai 2 local setup guide . What you can do A third person in the room. Bring Jarvis into an ongoing conversation with friends, talk through a problem aloud, or ask it to weigh in on a decision. “Jarvis, what do you think?” draws on the recent discussion, not just that one sentence. Remember beyond one session. Ask about past conversations, preferences and plans. Browse your local diary and knowledge graph in the Memory Viewer. Get things done. Built-in tools cover web search, weather, time, screenshot OCR, file access, optional search across your text and Markdown folders, nutrition tracking and optional location awareness. Connect your own tools. MCP servers add browser automation, smart-home controls and other integrations. Dictate into other apps. Hold a hotkey, speak, then release to paste locally transcribed text. See the platform limitations first. Type when you need to. The companion chat shares your voice conversation and memory. Text replies are silent, and you can rewind a sent message to regenerate from that point. Optional background work. Enable Background Tasks in Settings to queue work locally, follow results and cancel requests. Off by default. Bring Jarvis into the discussion You: We could have a picnic tomorrow. A friend: Depends on the weather. Should we plan something indoors instead? You: Jarvis, what do you think? Jarvis can use the recent conversation to understand that you are asking about the weather for the picnic, rather than treating the last sentence as an isolated question. This is the experience it is built around. Personalised requests can also draw on saved conversation history when no external tools are needed. How reliably it understands the context depends on speech recognition and your chosen model; see the evaluation results . Inside Jarvis Keep setup, activity and settings within reach. A guided start Choose the runtime that fits your machine. Setup walks through local models, speech and optional capabilities without requiring you to edit a configuration file. Progress you can actually follow The activity timeline keeps ordinary events readable. Downloads have a separate card with transferred bytes, percentage, speed and remaining time when the downloader provides them. Loading and warmup are distinct stages. Your setup, without the JSON Choose models, tune speech recognition, configure tools and enable Low Power Mode from Settings in the tray menu. A quiet companion to voice Open Chat for silent replies in the same conversation. Pause Voice Listening stops room transcription during meetings while chat and dictation stay available. Known limitations Jarvis is developed primarily on macOS. Windows and Linux behaviour may differ. See the evaluation results for tested capabilities. Accuracy and speed depend on your models and hardware. Smaller models can miss parts of complex requests, and slow speech recognition can drop utterances. Dictation is unavailable on macOS 26+ ( #172 ). Linux dictation requires X11, with limited Wayland support. Spoken “stop” can be mistaken for echo while Jarvis is speaking ( #24 ). No mobile app is available ( #17 ). Configuration Most people can use Settings from the tray. Advanced setups can edit ~/.config/jarvis/config.json . Open the configuration guide → The guide covers local model servers, speech recognition, Low Power Mode, voices, dictation, location, MCP integrations and troubleshooting. Dictation at a glance Platform Default hotkey Windows Ctrl + Win macOS, where supported Ctrl + Option Linux Ctrl + Alt Hold to record and release to paste. Double-tap for hands-free recording. Optional filler-word removal, a custom dictionary and dictation history are available in Settings. macOS needs Accessibility permission; Linux requires X11, with limited Wayland support. Bring your own tools Connect MCP servers for browser automation, Home Assistant, GitHub, databases and more. Credentials and network access depend on the tools you choose. Review a server's permissions before enabling it. Integration examples and server settings → Troubleshooting 🔇 Speech output unavailable: A voice-model or dependency failure disables speech output for the current run. Check the reason in Logs, correct the voice model settings or missing dependencies, then restart Jarvis. 🔊 Piper download interruptions: Connection resets and timeouts receive bounded retries. If they persist, check connectivity and restart Jarvis; completed voice files are retained. Certificate errors require correcting the trust configuration. 📥 Whisper download failures: Faster-whisper downloads run in a separate process with a five-minute limit. If a download crashes or times out, restart Jarvis to resume it; cached models stay available offline. 🎤 Whisper cache errors: Jarvis attempts one clean download recovery per startup. If it fails, check connectivity and free disk space, then follow the printed cache guidance and restart. Device fallbacks retain files downloaded during recovery.

others.title: Cadence: Taming Coupled Contention in Disaggregated Agent Clouds
others.abstract: Cadence targets multi-tenant LLM serving over operator-declared phases on disaggregated GPU pools and remote KV/cache tiers. We assume a small phase taxonomy—retrieval, tool fan-out, structured parsing, and decode—and adapt resource parameters within each phase online, rather than discovering arbitrary new behaviors at runtime. Despite strong single-tenant optimizations, clusters miss tail-latency SLOs once multi-phase requests collide with co-tenant bursts across GPU, cache, and network. The core challenge is coupled contention: a scheduler that only balances GPU utilization can still create cache hot spots and cross-rack fan-out, while transport-only fixes cannot prevent cache thrash or admission overload. Cadence jointly allocates GPU compute, KV/cache residency, and network bandwidth for phase-structured requests under per-tenant SLO and fairness constraints. It combines phase-aware resource contracts, an online co-scheduler for placement/cache/bandwidth bundles, and guardrails that combine admission control with cache and network enforcement. Across a 32-GPU, 400 Gbps leaf–spine testbed running four templates with eight tenants, at 90% offered load Cadence reduces P99 latency by 1.4–1.8 × vs GPU-Only and cuts SLO violations by 6.0–7.6 × vs GPU-Only (5.1–7.1 × vs Cache-Only/Net-Only); at the GPU-Only saturation point (100% normalized offered load), it improves cluster goodput by up to 54%. Cadence remains stable under 50% tenant churn and 40% retrieval skew, maintains Jain’s fairness index ≥ 0.84 at full load, and incurs 2.25% total CPU overhead in the control plane. The supplemental artifact includes the code, configurations, and scripts needed to reproduce the figures and tables.

others.title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems
others.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.

others.title: MosaicKV: SLO-Aware KV-Cache Virtualization for Multi-Tenant LLM Serving in the Cloud
others.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving has become a first-class cloud workload. The dominant cost driver is no longer compute alone. The key-value (KV) cache consumes tens of gigabytes per replica. It forces providers to either over-provision GPU memory or reject long-context requests. Existing high-throughput engines largely optimize within a single server. They assume KV stays resident in GPU HBM. Under multi-tenancy, HBM is routinely oversubscribed. Naive offloading (e.g., CUDA Unified Memory paging) then creates severe p99 TTFT spikes. These spikes break service-level objectives (SLOs). This paper presents MosaicKV, a KV-cache virtualization layer for multi-tenant LLM inference on shared GPU servers. MosaicKV exposes KV as a schedulable and migratable resource. It jointly optimizes GPU-memory partitioning across tenants. It decides which KV pages stay on HBM versus spill to host DRAM. It also times prefetch and micro-batching to hide PCIe DMA transfer latency. The key insight is that decoding has a predictable layer-by-layer access pattern. By co-designing page layout with a slack-aware scheduler, MosaicKV turns KV offload from reactive paging into a planned pipeline. On an 8-GPU server (8 × H100 SXM 80 GB) serving Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-32B, and Mixtral-8x7B under a 64-tenant mixed workload, MosaicKV improves goodput-under-SLO by 1.93–2.31 × under the same SLO contract (p99 TTFT ≤ 400 ms for interactive tenants; p99 completion ≤ 2 s for best-effort tenants) while reducing peak HBM KV footprint by 38%. Under flash-crowd bursts, MosaicKV keeps interactive-tenant p99 TTFT at 378–386 ms (within SLO). Unified Memory spikes to 1,055 ms (∼ 2.6 × SLO). MosaicKV achieves these gains without model changes. Runtime overhead remains modest (2.9–6.2%). This enables operators to safely run long-context and bursty tenants on shared GPU fleets.

others.title: Evaluating Agentic Systems Across the Lifecycle: A Taxonomy of Drifts and Success Criteria
others.abstract: Benchmarks like SWE-bench evaluate agents by checking whether a code patch passes a test suite. But what do you do when there is no test suite—when a “correct” investigation can take dozens of valid paths through 108 tools, and the only judge is an experienced engineer? This is the reality for enterprise agentic systems deployed in domains like site reliability engineering, where the unique combination of agent, model, tools, and business context makes general-purpose benchmarks inapplicable. We present a framework for evaluating such systems across their full lifecycle. We propose three complementary evaluation methods: a static validator that checks deterministic rules against agent traces (zero LLM cost, 34% pass rate on our corpus), a sub-agent auditor that uses an LLM to judge a structured summary (4.4K tokens/eval, 89% pass rate), and an observer agent that analyzes the full execution trace (8.2K tokens/eval, 74% pass rate). Majority-vote consensus across the three yields a 74% pass rate with zero cases of complete disagreement. We systematize six categories of drift that cause validated agents to degrade in production—model, prompt, tool availability, scope of access, third-party systems, and success criteria—and define detection and response strategies for each. We validate on a production SRE agent swarm with 108 tools across seven operational domains (Kubernetes, MongoDB, ArgoCD, Grafana, Temporal, JFrog, YugabyteDB), processing 53 alerts spanning 9 categories.

others.title: Memory-Decoupled Layer-Wise Fine-Tuning for Efficient On-Device LLM Adaptation
others.abstract: Federated Fine-Tuning (FFT) is essential for customizing Large Language Models (LLMs) at the edge while preserving data privacy. However, its scalability is severely constrained by the memory bottleneck. Our analysis reveals that the massive static memory footprint of LLM parameters exceeds the physical capacity of edge devices, rendering standard end-to-end training infeasible. In this paper, we propose EdgeLLM, a Cloud-Edge memory management system that democratizes efficient edge LLM adaptation via progressive layer training. Specifically, EdgeLLM re-architects the training process into a sequential pipeline: it dynamically manages the device memory hierarchy by maintaining only a minimal granular subset of layers on-chip while aggressively offloading inactive ones. To maximize system efficiency and convergence stability, EdgeLLM integrates four key components: (1) Resource Scheduler, which continuously probes device runtime memory availability to maximize resource utilization via dynamic workload mapping; (2) Training Coordinator, which bridges the semantic gap caused by offloading via virtualized context synthesis, ensuring coherent feature learning without full-graph residence; (3) Execution Planner, which optimizes the computation path by intelligently pruning redundancy and prioritizing task-critical layers for targeted adaptation; and (4) I/O Manager, which neutralizes the layer-swapping overhead through asynchronous prefetching and eviction. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that EdgeLLM effectively breaks the memory wall, unlocking participation for resource-constrained devices previously excluded from the training cohort. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, EdgeLLM delivers up to 11.86% performance improvement, accelerates model convergence by 2.08 × , and reduces communication overhead by 1.78 ×.

others.title: Familiar-Other Framing: Can Framing Project Pre-Existing Relationships with Familiar Others onto Dialogue Systems?
others.abstract: With recent advancements in large language models, the development of dialogue systems that imitate specific individuals has progressed, allowing users to project their impressions of the target person onto the system designed to imitate someone with whom they have a relationship, referred to as a familiar other. However, the impact of framing alone—informing users that the system is imitating a familiar other—on user impressions of the system remains unclear. To investigate this, we conducted an evaluation using a course support dialogue system. The results revealed that among students who rated their relationship with the course instructor highly, framing enhanced the perception of the system as a familiar other, even in a system that did not incorporate utterance imitation.

others.title: “I Can Talk to AI, but the Making Is Mine” Professional Artists’ Use of Generative Agents for Creative Work
others.abstract: Survey research finds that professional visual artists overwhelmingly dislike generative AI, yet many encounter it in their working lives. We interviewed five professional visual artists working across physical and digital media about where in the creative process they use a generative agent, how they use it, and why they use it in some phases and not others. We mapped the interviews onto the four phases of Mace and Ward’s model of the creative process. Participants used the agent only for gathering information within artwork conception and for developing ideas, and they kept idea conception, making, and finishing to themselves, citing authorship, craft, and the fear of feeding the model. We offer this account as a record of how professional artists place a generative agent while capabilities and norms are still taking shape.

others.title: A Concept of a Dialogue System Using a Stereotypical Mental Model of Others
others.abstract: In order for Large Language Models to communicate smoothly with humans, it is necessary to read “unstated intentions”—intentions that are not explicitly expressed in the interlocutor’s utterances. Previous studies proposed dialogue systems that respond while inferring the interlocutor’s unstated intentions; however, the beliefs and desires that form the basis of these intentions were fixed regardless of the interlocutor. In this study, we propose a dialogue system that sets predefined stereotypical Mental Models of Others for each assumed interlocutor type and generates responses by switching to the appropriate model based on the interlocutor’s utterances.

others.title: Shared View, Different Readings: Human–AI Alignment in Place Interpretation for XR Agents
others.abstract: AI agents in smart glasses and XR devices may share users’ views yet interpret places differently. In this study, we compared interpretations from 12 participants and Gemini 3.1 Pro across twelve places using matched field-of-view recordings. Compared with disagreement among humans, human–AI gaps were larger for place meaning and important cues; no additional gap was detected for place function or activity contexts. AI ratings tracked human patterns across scenes but varied less and showed little correspondence with individual differences within the same scene. These findings position functional judgments as tentative defaults but call for greater care with place meanings, cues, and individual impressions.

others.title: Registers Have Rhythms: Crossing Speech Style with Reply Timing in an LLM Journaling Agent
others.abstract: An agent that answers instantly and is never away keeps the rhythm of a service desk, seating its user as a customer. A register is indexed across several channels, so a peer relationship may require congruence between speech and timing. We demonstrate a local-LLM journaling agent implementing ma, the meaningful interval between turns, through a stochastic delay, a deferred read receipt, per-sentence message bursts, and push notifications. Prior work studies a user waiting at the screen; withholding the receipt lets them leave. In a within-subject pilot (N = 5), Likert ratings tracked phase order, not condition; the condition difference appears in what participants said. Three of five raised the read receipt unprompted, in the vocabulary of interpersonal obligation, and two said the agent’s speech style constrained their writing. At the booth, visitors cross speech style with timing, including the incongruent pairings we could not run.

others.title: The Delegation Boundary: Willingness to Delegate to AI Agents Depends on Retained Override More Than on Domain
others.abstract: What people hand over to an AI agent has a boundary: a point at which advice becomes action taken on their behalf. We examine that distinction across six agent scenarios rated by 296 U.S. adults, analyzed as 3 (domain) × 2 (advisory versus substitutive). Advisory scenarios received higher ratings in each domain, with a larger partial η2 for scenario category than for domain (.465 versus.053). The contrast was positive in every subgroup examined, but domain-specific differences showed low internal consistency (α =.08), giving limited support for a single cross-domain tendency. Objective AI knowledge and awareness of model limitations were associated with overall willingness in opposite directions. These vignette contrasts do not isolate a causal effect of retained override.

others.title: The AI engagement paradox: algorithmic congruence and its inverted-U effect on tourist experience quality
others.abstract:
Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ).
 
 
 
 A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction.
 
 
 
 AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward.
 
 
 
 This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy.
 
 
 
 This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

others.title: Pick Your Poison: Effects of Miscalibrated AI Advice and Silent Updates on Reliance
others.abstract: In AI-assisted decision-making, achieving warranted trust is essential: users should follow accurate advice while rejecting wrong suggestions. But as LLM-based AI agents reshape decision support, such agents often display miscalibrated confidence – ranging from confidently incorrect hallucinations to overly non-committal hedging. To understand how this behavior and unannounced system changes impact user trust, we conducted a two-phase online study (N=90) evaluating advice-seeking and reliance after confidence calibration is silently updated. We found that users’ willingness to seek AI advice is driven overwhelmingly by their pre-existing (positive) attitudes toward AI, not by the system’s prior performance. However, once they actively consult the AI, their reliance is significantly higher if they previously encountered a confidently incorrect or a non-committal system rather than a calibrated baseline. This effect dampens over time, with qualitative insights showing how unannounced background changes can erode perceived quality. These findings demonstrate that safe AI integration requires addressing individual user biases and transparently communicating updates.

others.title: Human Oversight in Agentic AI: Explainability, Anthropomorphism, and the Boundary of Cognitive Forcing
others.abstract: Explainability helps users assess evidence behind an AI recommendation, but it may not change decisions when that evidence goes unexamined. The problem is sharper in agentic decision support, where one assistant interprets evidence, explains its assessment, and recommends an action, while anthropomorphic delivery may add social credibility. Cognitive forcing, operationalised here as Human Intervention Checkpoints (HICs), requires users to specify what the assistant should examine before it recommends. We report a randomised 2 × 2 × 2 hiring experiment (N = 211) in which recruiters assessed a candidate whose unmet role-critical requirements were stated in every recommendation. Advancement was not associated with explanatory provenance, anthropomorphic delivery, HIC presence, or opening source documents. Post-task perceived explainability was associated with perceived anthropomorphism and trust, and trust was associated with advancement. In HIC-present conditions, 70 participants directed the assistant to a role-critical requirement and received Hold, yet 46 advanced. The findings identify a boundary of cognitive forcing: influence over what the agent evaluated and recommended did not reliably carry through to the final human decision.

others.title: Surgical Suppression of LLM Sycophancy via Sparse Autoencoder Feature Intervention
others.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy: they bend analyses toward a user’s stated preference rather than maintain an objective stance, undermining their value as decision-support agents in human–agent interaction. We propose a fine-grained intervention that suppresses sycophantic behavior without retraining. Using a pre-trained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) on the residual stream of gemma-2-9b-it, we decompose hidden states into sparse interpretable features. Candidate sycophancy features are selected by combining a gradient-based importance score with a sycophancy-specificity log-ratio and removed at inference time via zero-ablation. On the SycophancyEval Feedback benchmark, intervening at layer 31 reduces the sycophancy rate from \(41.0\%\) to \(34.8\%\) (p < 0.001, McNemar), turns \(34.7\%\) of originally sycophantic responses neutral, and improves fluency. The effect transfers to held-out prompts, consistent with a substantial part of sycophancy being mediated by a small set of late-layer features, and suggesting sparse features as a runtime control surface for keeping interactive agents objective.

others.title: “I check it when it feels wrong” – Computer Science Student Usage and Perspectives on AI Chatbots
others.abstract: We present a qualitative interview study with 17 Canadian computer science and software engineering undergraduates exploring their self-initiated, unsupervised AI chatbot use. We find that most participants, despite being CS students often assumed to have stronger technical intuitions, lacked an accurate understanding of how generative AI produces output. This miscalibration was associated with plausibility-based fact-checking: participants who described genAI as a retrieval or database system had no reliable trigger for verifying confidently-stated misinformation. We discuss implications for AI literacy education and human-AI interaction design.

others.title: AutoPrompt: A Real-Time Multimodal Agent for Closed-Loop Interaction through Generative Visuals in Live Performance
others.abstract: Recent advances in multi-agentic AI enables the interaction of multiple specialised AI agents rather than a single general-purpose AI. However, there has been little exploration of how this can be used within the creative community. We present AutoPrompt, a real-time multimodal agent that perceives a performer’s vocal and visual expression and generates prompts for a generative visual system, forming a closed perception-action loop in live performance. We tested AutoPrompt with two professional dancers during a workshop where their movement, language and emotions influenced live AI-generated visuals. Through this workshop we identified which modalities and mechanisms support creative expression and explored the benefits and limitations of the system, laying the groundwork for future work to examine how multi-agent AI can be better integrated into the creative arts.

others.title: Predict Me if You Can: Simulating User Responses with Synthetic Data: Evaluating the Fidelity of LLM-Based Synthetic Respondents
others.abstract: Conditioning language models on persona profiles is standard practice for generating synthetic survey responses, yet the relative contribution of different attributes to the fidelity of synthetic survey responses has not been systematically quantified. To test this, we conditioned four large language models (LLMs) on profiles of 258 employed South Korean adults surveyed on AI-related job replacement risk. We grouped 11 attributes into three blocks (demographics, socioeconomic position & ideology, experience) and evaluated four cumulative levels of persona richness. A leave-one-out ablation identified the most impactful block. Fidelity generally rose with richer personas, and ablation showed that only experience-related attributes contributed meaningfully, while demographic attributes were net-neutral at best. For human-agent interaction (HAI) research with synthetic respondents, fidelity hinges on attribute relevance, not information quantity — neither the largest model nor all attributes maximize it.

others.title: Gradis:A Human–AI Collaborative Framework for Workforce-Aligned Curriculum Generation and Personalized Learning
others.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and evolving workforce requirements have widened the gap between traditional educational curricula and industry needs. Recent developments in large language models (LLMs) and intelligent tutoring systems have improved curriculum generation and personalized learning experiences. However, most existing solutions remain focused on isolated educational tasks and lack a unified framework that integrates workforce intelligence, organizational knowledge, human expertise, and adaptive learning. This paper proposes Gradis, a human–AI collaborative framework for workforce-aligned curriculum generation and personalized learning. Gradis integrates organizational knowledge, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and human expert validation to support the generation and expert-guided refinement of adaptive curricula in response to changing industry needs. Unlike fully automated educational systems, Gradis positions human experts as key decision-makers throughout the curriculum lifecycle while leveraging AI to improve scalability, efficiency, and personalization.

others.title: Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies
others.abstract: As social agents, robots, conversational AI systems, and virtual characters become embedded in everyday environments, HAI is shifting from isolated one-human/one-agent interaction toward socially embedded multi-person and multi-agent settings. This workshop explores how trust, blame, and responsibility emerge, become distributed, and are negotiated among users, agents, developers, institutions, bystanders, and broader social contexts. We focus on agents as social participants in complex environments, including group dynamics, psychological safety, agent refusal, moral consideration, and legal or governance questions. The workshop aims to develop a preliminary issue map, research agenda, and interdisciplinary network for socially sustainable human-agent societies.

others.title: Exploring How Anthropomorphism and Autonomy Affect Users’ Politeness Toward AI Chatbots in Psychological Support Contexts
others.abstract: The Media Equation Theory, proposed in the last century, suggests that people tend to respond politely to computers mindlessly, as they would to humans. In the generative AI era, however, both the forms of user interaction interfaces and the usage contexts of AI have evolved significantly. This prompts us to revisit the classic theory and conduct more nuanced studies to reexamine it. Specifically, we explore users’ politeness toward AI chatbots in the context of psychological support through two controlled experiments, focusing on two factors marginalized by the Media Equation Theory: anthropomorphism and autonomy. Study 1 examined the effects of anthropomorphism and perceived autonomy on users’ self-reported politeness toward chatbots through a human-chatbot conversation experiment. Study 2 incorporated gender as an additional variable and conducted a follow-up experiment. Results showed that chatbots’ appearance anthropomorphism negatively predicted users’ politeness, whereas perceived autonomy positively predicted users’ politeness. Follow-up interviews further indicated that politeness toward AI chatbots follows a different logic from the mindlessness proposed by the Media Equation Theory, revealing the paradoxical coexistence of users’ conscious awareness of AI’s non-human nature and their expectations for human-like capabilities. Overall, this work seeks to extend the classic theory in human-AI interaction and provide implications for the design of AI chatbots.

others.title: From Perceived Trust to Delegation in Agentic AI: Reliability, Apparent Bistability, and Delegation Thresholds
others.abstract: Trust is central to human–agent interaction, but agentic AI raises a stronger question: when does perceived trust translate into delegated action? This poster introduces an agent-based simulation in which agents delegate when trust exceeds a threshold, observe success or failure, and update trust through outcome feedback with tunable failure sensitivity. We vary AI reliability and delegation thresholds while examining social conformity and failure sensitivity. Results show that unreliable systems drive abandonment, while intermediate regimes can produce apparent bistability: identical AI reliability can lead to adoption or rejection depending on initial trust and the delegation threshold. Conformity can sustain delegation by preventing isolated trust collapse. These findings suggest that delegation thresholds act as control parameters for sustained reliance. Future work will validate the model with human participants and heterogeneous agent profiles and tasks.

others.title: Sincerity or Treasure: Bounded Strategic Communication Gameplay with LLM Agent
others.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents enable new forms of human-agent interaction by supporting flexible reasoning and natural language communication. However, unrestricted interaction often makes agent behavior difficult to understand and strategically engage with. This work presents Sincerity or Treasure, an AI-native strategy game that investigates how humans influence an LLM agent through bounded strategic communication. In the game, players interact with Jesika, an LLM-driven character, by selectively revealing limited clues and adding natural-language framing. Instead of treating language as simple dialogue, the game makes information selection and linguistic framing strategic actions. A preliminary study with 26 participants shows that players adapted their communication strategies through deception, trust management, and adjustment of expression. These findings suggest that bounded strategic communication can create meaningful gameplay and interaction space where an agent's reasoning process becomes a central component of game system.

others.title: Simulating Mutual Subjectivity: An Agent-Based Framework with LLM-Generated Dual-Perspective Reports for Tethered Side-by-Side Walking
others.abstract: Two people walking side by side negotiate direction continuously, with neither fully leading nor following. This paper presents a prototype simulation framework for studying such mutual subjectivity in tethered side-by-side walking. Two agents joined by an ON/OFF tether are each governed by a Self-Fulfillment Drive and a Relatedness Drive, and a large language model (LLM) generates pseudo-subjective reports from both perspectives. In an illustrative run, the agent configured for high relatedness read a slack tether as separation — inverting the semantics the model assigns to that state. Because the error tracks the very parameter the framework exists to vary, we argue it is a structural hazard for any use of LLMs to voice simulated agent state, not merely an underspecified prompt.

others.title: Autonomy of Boundedly Rational Agents in Dyadic Interactions
others.abstract: AI agents now work alongside people in domains ranging from autonomous vehicles to conversational systems. A recurring question is when an agent’s behavior counts as self-determined rather than merely reactive to its human partner. This matters for ethical conduct, which is widely argued to require some form of autonomy. Yet, its computational meaning is rarely made precise. In this paper, we study an agent’s autonomy in dyadic interactions, measured by the extent to which the agent’s behavior is explained by its own state rather than by its partner’s signals. This quantity captures information-theoretic self-determination as inferred from interaction traces. We characterize autonomy as a function of how deterministically the agent acts, how strongly it optimizes payoffs, and how much past interaction it retains. Using analytical and numerical results from four distinct games, we find that autonomy peaks at high but sub-maximal determinism and is dissociable from rationality. All four settings achieve the same level of autonomy regardless of the agent’s payoff disposition, so rationality never raises the ceiling. What the payoff structure determines is the direction in which rationality trades against determinism. Payoff-seeking play economizes on determinism in one setting, payoff-avoiding play in another, and neither matters where the agent cannot influence its payoff. Our results suggest design principles for interactive agents that remain consistent and self-determined.

others.title: A Real-time Multimodal Adaptive Mixed Reality System for Procedural Task Guidance
others.abstract: Procedural tasks often require users to interpret instructions, monitor task progress, and recover from errors while interacting with physical objects. Mixed reality (MR) can support such tasks by presenting guidance directly within the user’s workspace. However, providing effective assistance remains challenging as user behavior, task progress, and support requirements may vary. We present a real-time multimodal adaptive MR system for procedural task guidance that integrates semantic task tracking, user-state estimation, and adaptive assistance within a unified closed-loop architecture. The system represents procedures as dependency-aware task graphs, continuously tracks task progress , and estimates procedural difficulty from gaze, hand, and head-motion signals. These signals are used to dynamically adapt guidance content, timing, and presentation through an LLM-based assistance module. We implemented the system on Microsoft HoloLens 2 and evaluated it through technical validation and a user study involving 20 participants performing procedural tasks of varying complexity. Results demonstrate robust closed-loop operation, achieving an action-recognition F1 score of 0.97 and 100% step-completion accuracy. User study results indicate that adaptive guidance reduced procedural difficulties and recovery time following task deviations, particularly during more complex procedures.

others.title: How Does Multi-Agent System Architecture Shape Human-Agent Interaction in Long-Horizon Strategic Tasks?
others.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used in tasks requiring coordination, yet existing benchmarks provide limited support for long-horizon studies involving both humans and alternative MAS organizations. We present an agent-agnostic, turn-based strategic simulation for comparing four organizational configurations within a common protocol. The environment combines simultaneous planning, partial observability, territorial competition, and text-based diplomacy. We outline two planned evaluations: AI-only simulations and mixed sessions with two MAS-controlled and four human-controlled players. Outcomes include strategic performance, communication patterns, computational cost, and post-session trust. Because the configurations differ in decision authority, observation scope, communication, and diplomacy, the study compares complete organizational configurations rather than isolated architectural factors. The framework provides a basis for controlled studies of long-term Human-Agent Interaction.

others.title: Integrating a Multi-Tier Memory Manager into a Educational RAG System
others.abstract: Large language model agents often perform well within one conversation yet do not persist interaction-derived state, procedures, and user context needed for sustained collaboration when the session ends. This paper presents the integration of a memory-first extension to a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agent, in which memory is treated as an explicit architectural layer rather than an enlarged chat history. The current prototype implements a Memory Core and Memory Manager for persistent conversational, semantic, procedural, and episodic memory. At the same time, the complete memory-aware architecture and its evaluation protocol are presented as ongoing work. Relational tables preserve conversational events, while vector-enabled SQL tables store embedded memory units enriched with timestamps, source, intent, confidence, and lifecycle metadata. Deterministic and agent-triggered operations support read, write, update, and delete operations and context-window segmentation. The proposed interface is designed to expose the memory type and provenance associated with retrieved information. The work reframes agent memory as both an engineering and a human-agent interaction problem: useful persistence requires not only accurate recall, but also transparent, controllable, and correctable remembering.

others.title: Just an AI: How Do Humans Respond to LLM Disclosure?
others.abstract: Disclosure of AI limitations, knowledge, and underlying architecture is a transparency mechanism that helps users calibrate expectations and trust-related behavior. However, it is unclear how users respond to such disclosures. We qualitatively analyzed 336 LLM disclosure segments from publicly accessible naturalistic human-LLM conversations. We coded LLM disclosure types, along with their preceding human triggers and subsequent human responses. For human responses, we found that explicit acceptance of LLM disclosure is rare, regardless of the trigger or disclosure type. Instead, users tend to explore further or redirect to a new topic. When users object, they do not object to the disclosure’s informative value but to its repetitive, formulaic delivery. We discuss implications for designing and operationalizing the efficiency of LLM disclosures as transparency mechanisms.
